caption:
US officials believe Alice Huang, an executive at NVIDIA customer Megaspeed, is a Chinese intelligence asset who built a close tie to Jensen Huang, The New York Times reported.
Officials did not believe Huang knew of her role. NVIDIA called his contacts with her "not unusual or unexpected."
No one has been charged, and Megaspeed has hired outside counsel.

Should tech CEOs be warned when spies target them?

paragraphs.text: US officials believe that Alice Huang, a senior executive at the Singapore based data center company Megaspeed, is a Chinese intelligence asset who built a close relationship with Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in order to pass information to Beijing, The New York Times reported on October 29, 2026. The account below is based on summaries of that report by the Free Press Journal and AI Weekly.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen. She and Jensen Huang are not related. According to the report, US surveillance of her led officials to conclude that she was an intelligence asset, and it also captured her contacts with an American citizen whom officials later identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as unmasking.
The chips at the center of the case

US agencies had already suspected Megaspeed of helping China obtain advanced Nvidia chips. Trade records cited by the Times show that the company's Malaysian sister company bought at least $4.8 billion of advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026. Megaspeed supplies computing power to Chinese companies, including Alibaba, and investigators suspect that some of the chips reached China illegally. The Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed was handed to the Justice Department earlier this year, according to the report.

Megaspeed has been under scrutiny for more than a year. Tom's Hardware reported in October 2025 that the company was created in 2023 as an offshore unit of 7Road, a Chinese gaming and cloud firm with state backed investors, and that it had committed to buy about $2 billion of Nvidia GPUs, including H100 and H800 models. At the time, Nvidia said its own checks had found the company legally qualified, with no signs that chips had been diverted.
What officials did and did not do

President Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago and chose not to act, the Times reported, because he was wary of disrupting Nvidia's sales and complicating trade relations with China. Officials at the time did not believe Jensen Huang knew of Alice Huang's role, although some senior administration officials doubt that he could have been unaware. According to the report, he has not received the defensive briefing that is sometimes given to people targeted by foreign intelligence services, and surveillance of Alice Huang is continuing.

The report also described Jensen Huang's ties to the administration. Nvidia gave at least $20 million to the president's ballroom fund, and Huang sat at the head table at last month's state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Officials told the Times that his closeness to the president has slowed efforts to crack down on Nvidia, and that some Commerce Department probes and proposed sanctions have stalled.

An Nvidia spokesman told the Times that Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were "not unusual or unexpected" and that meeting customers is part of his job. Nvidia said it believes the government would warn it of any threat, that Megaspeed receives ordinary business information rather than sensitive trade secrets, and that it has found no evidence of smuggling. Nvidia still lists Megaspeed as a cloud partner. Megaspeed said it takes the allegations seriously and has hired outside counsel to conduct an internal investigation. No one has been charged in connection with the allegations.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the report moves the long running debate over Nvidia chips reaching China from a question of trade rules to a question of national security. Its central claims come from unnamed officials and have not been tested in court, which leaves a wide gap between suspicion and proof.
Watch whether the Justice Department's Megaspeed investigation produces charges, and whether Congress asks Nvidia to explain how it vets the customers that buy its most advanced chips.
